mentioned_issues.body:
## Original Request

> add red background to app

## User Story

As a developer/stakeholder on Boykai's Tech Connect, I want the application to have a red background so that the visual theme and branding of the app reflects the intended design direction. This change should apply consistently across the application's primary background surfaces.

## UI/UX Description

The application's primary background should be updated to a red color. The specific red shade should be defined using a design token or CSS variable (e.g., a brand red such as #FF0000, #E53E3E, or a Tailwind red like `red-600`) to ensure consistency and easy future updates. The red background must maintain sufficient contrast ratios (WCAG AA minimum 4.5:1) against all overlaid text and UI components. All existing foreground elements — text, cards, modals, buttons, icons — should be reviewed and adjusted if needed to remain legible against the new background. The background change should apply globally across all pages and routes, and must be responsive across mobile, tablet, and desktop viewports.

## Functional Requirements

- System MUST update the application's global/root background color to red using a defined color token or CSS variable for maintainability.
- System MUST ensure the chosen red background color meets WCAG AA contrast requirements (minimum 4.5:1 ratio) against all primary text and interactive elements.
- System MUST apply the red background consistently across all pages, routes, and views within the application.
- System MUST NOT break or obscure any existing UI components (buttons, cards, modals, navigation, forms) when the background color is applied.
- System SHOULD define the red color value as a reusable design token or CSS custom property (e.g., --color-background: #E53E3E) to allow easy future theme changes.
- System SHOULD verify the background color renders correctly across major browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) and on mobile viewports.
- System MUST update or replace any hardcoded background colors in component-level styles that would conflict with the new global red background.
- System SHOULD include a visual regression check or screenshot comparison to confirm the background change does not introduce unintended UI side effects.

## Technical Notes

Implement the red background by setting the background-color on the root element (e.g., body, #app, or .app-container) using a CSS custom property or design token so it cascades globally. If the project uses a design system or theming library (e.g., Tailwind CSS, styled-components, MUI ThemeProvider), update the theme's background token rather than applying inline styles. Ensure z-index layering and any existing white/light background overrides on child components are audited and updated. Add the color change to the global stylesheet or theme config file to keep it centralized and easy to revert or iterate on.

closing_issues.title: Perform Deep Security Review and Harden Application Code
closing_issues.body:
## Overview
Conduct a thorough security audit of the application, identifying and remediating vulnerabilities using industry best practices. All fixes should maintain clean, simple, and DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) code principles to avoid introducing new complexity or duplication.

## Technical Details
- Review authentication and authorization flows for weaknesses (e.g., broken access control, privilege escalation)
- Audit input validation and sanitization to guard against injection attacks (SQL, XSS, command injection, etc.)
- Check secrets management — ensure no hardcoded credentials, API keys, or tokens exist in the codebase or GitHub Workflows configs
- Review dependency tree for known CVEs using tools such as `npm audit`, `Dependabot`, or `Snyk`
- Inspect GitHub Workflow YAML files for insecure patterns (e.g., use of `pull_request_target`, unpinned actions, excessive permissions)
- Evaluate data exposure risks in API responses, logs, and error messages
- Consolidate any duplicated security logic (e.g., repeated auth checks, validation routines) into shared utilities following DRY principles
- Reference OWASP Top 10 and GitHub Actions security hardening guides as baseline standards

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All critical and high severity vulnerabilities identified and remediated
- [ ] GitHub Workflow files follow least-privilege permissions and use pinned action versions
- [ ] No hardcoded secrets or sensitive data found in source code or workflow configs
- [ ] Duplicated security logic refactored into reusable, well-tested shared modules
- [ ] A security findings report is documented summarizing issues found, fixes applied, and any accepted risks

closing_issues.title: Increase Meaningful Test Coverage, Fix Discovered Bugs, and Enforce DRY Best Practices
closing_issues.body:
**User Story:**
As a developer maintaining this application, I want comprehensive, meaningful test coverage aligned with the documented intended functionality so that regressions are caught early, discovered bugs are permanently resolved, and the codebase remains reliable and maintainable. I need all tests to follow best practices, remain DRY, and be simple enough to serve as living documentation of expected behavior.

**Requirements:**
- System MUST audit the existing test suite and remove or rewrite any tests that do not align with documented intended app functionality (e.g., tests that assert incorrect behavior, test implementation details rather than outcomes, or provide false confidence).
- System MUST add new tests for all critical application flows and features described in the project documentation that currently lack coverage, ensuring each test validates real, user-facing or system-level behavior.
- System MUST identify, reproduce, and fix all bugs and issues discovered during the testing audit, with each bug fix accompanied by a dedicated regression test to prevent reintroduction.
- System MUST follow DRY principles in the test suite by extracting shared setup, fixtures, mocks, and helper utilities into reusable modules rather than duplicating logic across test files.
- System MUST follow testing best practices including clear Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) structure, descriptive test names that communicate intent, isolation of unit tests, and meaningful assertions with informative failure messages.
- System SHOULD achieve a meaningfully higher test coverage percentage after this work, targeting coverage of all documented core features, happy paths, and critical edge cases.
- System MUST ensure all new and existing tests pass consistently in CI without flakiness, and any previously skipped or broken tests are either fixed or explicitly removed with documented rationale.
- System SHOULD organize tests logically to mirror the application's structure, making it easy for future developers to locate tests corresponding to specific features or modules.

**Technical Notes:**
Begin with a full audit of existing tests against the project documentation to classify each test as meaningful, redundant, or misaligned — then prioritize additions by feature criticality. Use the project's established testing framework and conventions; introduce shared fixtures, factories, or test helpers to enforce DRY principles across the suite. For each discovered bug, write a failing regression test first (red), apply the fix (green), then refactor as needed. Ensure the CI pipeline enforces test passage on all PRs going forward to maintain the quality baseline established by this work.

mentioned_issues.title: Perform Deep Security Review and Harden Application Code
mentioned_issues.body:
## Overview
Conduct a thorough security audit of the application, identifying and remediating vulnerabilities using industry best practices. All fixes should maintain clean, simple, and DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) code principles to avoid introducing new complexity or duplication.

## Technical Details
- Review authentication and authorization flows for weaknesses (e.g., broken access control, privilege escalation)
- Audit input validation and sanitization to guard against injection attacks (SQL, XSS, command injection, etc.)
- Check secrets management — ensure no hardcoded credentials, API keys, or tokens exist in the codebase or GitHub Workflows configs
- Review dependency tree for known CVEs using tools such as `npm audit`, `Dependabot`, or `Snyk`
- Inspect GitHub Workflow YAML files for insecure patterns (e.g., use of `pull_request_target`, unpinned actions, excessive permissions)
- Evaluate data exposure risks in API responses, logs, and error messages
- Consolidate any duplicated security logic (e.g., repeated auth checks, validation routines) into shared utilities following DRY principles
- Reference OWASP Top 10 and GitHub Actions security hardening guides as baseline standards

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All critical and high severity vulnerabilities identified and remediated
- [ ] GitHub Workflow files follow least-privilege permissions and use pinned action versions
- [ ] No hardcoded secrets or sensitive data found in source code or workflow configs
- [ ] Duplicated security logic refactored into reusable, well-tested shared modules
- [ ] A security findings report is documented summarizing issues found, fixes applied, and any accepted risks

closing_issues.title: Add MCP Configuration Support for GitHub Agents in Settings Page
closing_issues.body:
**User Story:**
As a user authenticated via GitHub OAuth, I want to add and manage MCPs (Model Context Protocols) for GitHub agents directly from the Settings page so that I can customize and extend the capabilities of GitHub agents tied to my specific GitHub account.

**Requirements:**
- System MUST display an MCP management section within the existing Settings page, accessible only to authenticated users.
- System MUST use the user's GitHub OAuth login credentials to scope all MCP configurations to their specific GitHub account.
- System MUST allow users to add a new MCP by providing required configuration details (e.g., name, endpoint URL), and persist these settings linked to the authenticated GitHub account.
- System MUST display a list of all MCPs currently configured for the user's GitHub account, including each MCP's name and active status.
- System MUST allow users to remove an existing MCP from their GitHub account configuration, with a confirmation prompt before deletion.
- System MUST provide real-time inline feedback (success or error messages) after any add or remove operation, reflecting the result of the OAuth-scoped API call.
- System MUST show an appropriate empty state in the MCP list when no MCPs have been configured for the authenticated GitHub account.
- System SHOULD validate MCP input fields (e.g., non-empty name, valid URL format for endpoints) before submitting and surface validation errors inline.
- System MUST handle GitHub OAuth token expiration or permission errors gracefully, prompting re-authentication if necessary during MCP save operations.

**Technical Notes:**
MCP configurations should be stored server-side, keyed by the user's GitHub account ID retrieved from the GitHub OAuth token (via GitHub's /user API). Use the existing GitHub OAuth session/token infrastructure to authorize all MCP CRUD operations — ensure API routes for MCP management require a valid OAuth token with sufficient scopes. Consider a REST or GraphQL endpoint pattern like POST /api/settings/mcps, DELETE /api/settings/mcps/:id, and GET /api/settings/mcps scoped per GitHub user. On the frontend, use the existing Settings page component and extend it with a new MCP sub-section; manage async state with loading/error/success states. Ensure MCP endpoint URLs are sanitized server-side to prevent SSRF vulnerabilities.

closing_issues.title: Settings Page: Dynamic Value Fetching, Caching, and UX Simplification
closing_issues.body:
**User Story:**
As a user configuring the application, I want the Settings page to automatically retrieve and present valid option values (e.g., available GitHub Copilot models fetched directly from GitHub) as dynamic dropdowns, and I want the overall Settings page to be simplified so that important settings — model providers, chat models, GitHub agent models, and Signal connection — are easy to find and configure without clutter.

**Requirements:**
- System MUST automatically fetch valid option values from the appropriate external API (e.g., GitHub API for available Copilot/GitHub models) when a user selects a provider that supports dynamic enumeration, and populate the corresponding setting's dropdown with the retrieved values.
- System MUST cache fetched option values locally (e.g., in-memory or persistent storage) with a configurable TTL to minimize redundant API calls and respect provider rate limits; stale cache should trigger a background refresh, not a blocking fetch.
- System MUST display a loading indicator (spinner or skeleton) in the dropdown while remote values are being fetched, and must disable the dropdown during the initial load to prevent invalid selection.
- System MUST gracefully handle API fetch failures by showing a user-friendly error message within the dropdown area, providing a manual retry button, and falling back to previously cached values if available.
- System MUST NOT fetch external values if the required authentication or connection (e.g., GitHub credentials, Signal connection) is not configured; instead, it should prompt the user to complete the prerequisite setup with a clear inline message.
- System MUST apply rate-limit-aware request throttling and backoff when fetching dynamic values, and must surface a non-blocking warning to the user if the API rate limit is approached or exceeded.
- System MUST simplify the Settings page layout by prominently grouping and surfacing critical settings: model provider selection, chat model selection, GitHub agent model selection, and Signal connection configuration, while collapsing or reorganizing secondary/advanced settings.
- System SHOULD invalidate and refresh the cached values when the user changes a dependent setting (e.g., switching from GitHub Copilot to a different model provider) to ensure dropdowns always reflect the current provider's available options.
- System SHOULD display metadata about cached values (e.g., 'Last updated 5 minutes ago') adjacent to dynamically populated dropdowns so users understand the freshness of the options presented.
- System MUST ensure the Settings page and all dynamic dropdowns are fully accessible (ARIA labels, keyboard navigation, screen reader announcements for loading/error states) and responsive across screen sizes.

**Technical Notes:**
Implement a settings value resolver service/module that maps each setting field to a fetch strategy (static enum, remote API, or derived). For GitHub Copilot model lists, use the GitHub Models API or Copilot API endpoint (e.g., GET /models or equivalent) authenticated with the stored GitHub token; abstract this behind a provider interface so other future providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) can plug in easily. Use a cache layer (e.g., a Map with TTL metadata, or a lightweight persistent store like localStorage/IndexedDB or a backend KV store) keyed by provider+setting type; default TTL should be ~5–15 minutes with exponential backoff on rate-limit errors (respect Retry-After headers). For the UX simplification, audit all existing settings fields and categorize them as primary (model providers, chat models, GitHub agent models, Signal connection) vs. secondary/advanced — consider a collapsible 'Advanced' section to reduce visual noise. Ensure Settings state management is reactive so that changing a provider field immediately triggers a fetch for dependent dropdown fields.

mentioned_issues.title: Settings Page: Dynamic Value Fetching, Caching, and UX Simplification
mentioned_issues.body:
**User Story:**
As a user configuring the application, I want the Settings page to automatically retrieve and present valid option values (e.g., available GitHub Copilot models fetched directly from GitHub) as dynamic dropdowns, and I want the overall Settings page to be simplified so that important settings — model providers, chat models, GitHub agent models, and Signal connection — are easy to find and configure without clutter.

**Requirements:**
- System MUST automatically fetch valid option values from the appropriate external API (e.g., GitHub API for available Copilot/GitHub models) when a user selects a provider that supports dynamic enumeration, and populate the corresponding setting's dropdown with the retrieved values.
- System MUST cache fetched option values locally (e.g., in-memory or persistent storage) with a configurable TTL to minimize redundant API calls and respect provider rate limits; stale cache should trigger a background refresh, not a blocking fetch.
- System MUST display a loading indicator (spinner or skeleton) in the dropdown while remote values are being fetched, and must disable the dropdown during the initial load to prevent invalid selection.
- System MUST gracefully handle API fetch failures by showing a user-friendly error message within the dropdown area, providing a manual retry button, and falling back to previously cached values if available.
- System MUST NOT fetch external values if the required authentication or connection (e.g., GitHub credentials, Signal connection) is not configured; instead, it should prompt the user to complete the prerequisite setup with a clear inline message.
- System MUST apply rate-limit-aware request throttling and backoff when fetching dynamic values, and must surface a non-blocking warning to the user if the API rate limit is approached or exceeded.
- System MUST simplify the Settings page layout by prominently grouping and surfacing critical settings: model provider selection, chat model selection, GitHub agent model selection, and Signal connection configuration, while collapsing or reorganizing secondary/advanced settings.
- System SHOULD invalidate and refresh the cached values when the user changes a dependent setting (e.g., switching from GitHub Copilot to a different model provider) to ensure dropdowns always reflect the current provider's available options.
- System SHOULD display metadata about cached values (e.g., 'Last updated 5 minutes ago') adjacent to dynamically populated dropdowns so users understand the freshness of the options presented.
- System MUST ensure the Settings page and all dynamic dropdowns are fully accessible (ARIA labels, keyboard navigation, screen reader announcements for loading/error states) and responsive across screen sizes.

**Technical Notes:**
Implement a settings value resolver service/module that maps each setting field to a fetch strategy (static enum, remote API, or derived). For GitHub Copilot model lists, use the GitHub Models API or Copilot API endpoint (e.g., GET /models or equivalent) authenticated with the stored GitHub token; abstract this behind a provider interface so other future providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) can plug in easily. Use a cache layer (e.g., a Map with TTL metadata, or a lightweight persistent store like localStorage/IndexedDB or a backend KV store) keyed by provider+setting type; default TTL should be ~5–15 minutes with exponential backoff on rate-limit errors (respect Retry-After headers). For the UX simplification, audit all existing settings fields and categorize them as primary (model providers, chat models, GitHub agent models, Signal connection) vs. secondary/advanced — consider a collapsible 'Advanced' section to reduce visual noise. Ensure Settings state management is reactive so that changing a provider field immediately triggers a fetch for dependent dropdown fields.

closing_issues.title: Preserve Full User-Provided GitHub Issue Description Without Truncation
closing_issues.body:
**User Story:**
As a user composing a GitHub Issue via chat, I want my full issue description preserved and used verbatim — regardless of length — so that long, detailed descriptions are not silently truncated, ensuring the created GitHub Issue accurately reflects everything I wrote.

**Requirements:**
- System MUST detect when a user-provided GitHub Issue description exceeds any currently applied truncation threshold and use the full text instead of a shortened version.
- System MUST pass the complete, unmodified issue description text to the GitHub Issues API as the issue body, regardless of character or line count.
- System MUST NOT silently truncate, summarize, or shorten any user-provided issue description at any stage of processing — including intermediate chat handling, state storage, or API call construction.
- System MUST preserve all formatting in the full description including newlines, markdown syntax, bullet points, headers, and code blocks.
- System SHOULD notify the user explicitly if the GitHub API itself imposes a hard content length limit that prevents the full description from being submitted, rather than silently cutting the content.
- System MUST correctly handle descriptions of varying lengths — from single-line to multi-thousand-character inputs — without behavioral differences in content fidelity.
- System SHOULD be tested with edge-case inputs including descriptions at common truncation boundaries (e.g., 256, 1024, 4096, 65536 characters) to confirm no truncation occurs.
- System MUST store and forward the full description text through all intermediate processing steps (e.g., prompt construction, API payload building) without data loss.

**Technical Notes:**
Audit the chat-to-GitHub-issue pipeline to identify any point where the description string is sliced, capped, or passed through a truncating formatter — common culprits include LLM prompt construction (where descriptions may be trimmed to fit context windows), intermediate state serialization, or manual substring operations before the API call. The GitHub REST API for creating issues accepts a `body` field with up to 65,536 characters; ensure the full user text is placed directly into this field without modification. If the description is used inside an LLM prompt as context, separate the 'user description passthrough' path from the 'LLM reasoning' path so that AI summarization never affects the verbatim output. Add a unit test that creates an issue with a description at or near the GitHub API body limit and asserts the returned issue body matches the input exactly.

closing_issues.title: Add 'Human' Agent Type to Agent Pipeline with Sub-Issue Assignment and Completion Detection
closing_issues.body:
**User Story:**
As a pipeline creator, I want to add a 'Human' step to any Agent Pipeline column so that I can assign manual human tasks within automated workflows, tracked via GitHub Sub Issues assigned to the issue creator, and automatically continue the pipeline when the human marks their task complete.

**Requirements:**
- System MUST add 'Human' as a selectable option in the '+ Add Agent' dropdown/menu for every status column across all Agent Pipelines by default
- System MUST auto-create a GitHub Sub Issue for the Human step using the same sub-issue creation mechanism used for agent steps when a GitHub Issue containing a Human step is triggered
- System MUST automatically assign the generated Human Sub Issue to the user who created the parent GitHub Issue
- System MUST mark the Human step as complete and continue pipeline execution when the associated GitHub Sub Issue is closed
- System MUST mark the Human step as complete and continue pipeline execution when the user comments exactly 'Done!' on the GitHub Issue, matching the same completion-signaling pattern used by agents
- System MUST NOT advance the pipeline past the Human step until one of the two completion conditions (Sub Issue closed OR 'Done!' comment) is detected
- System SHOULD visually distinguish the Human agent card from automated agent cards in the pipeline UI (e.g., person icon, 'Human' label)
- System MUST support Human steps in any position within the pipeline sequence, ensuring steps after the Human step execute only after the Human step is complete
- System SHOULD handle edge cases where the issue creator cannot be resolved, surfacing a clear error or fallback assignment behavior
- System MUST apply the 'Human' agent option to all existing pipelines as well as any newly created pipelines without requiring manual reconfiguration

**Technical Notes:**
The Human step should hook into the existing sub-issue creation and pipeline-step-completion infrastructure — reuse the same Sub Issue creation logic used for agent steps, injecting the issue creator's GitHub username as the assignee at creation time. Completion detection requires a GitHub webhook listener (or polling mechanism) to watch for two events on the Sub Issue or parent Issue: (1) Sub Issue state change to 'closed', and (2) an IssueComment event on the parent Issue where the comment body exactly equals 'Done!' from the assigned user. The pipeline state machine should treat the Human step as a blocking async step, similar to how it awaits agent completion, resuming downstream steps only upon a completion event. Ensure idempotency so that if both completion conditions are triggered simultaneously, the pipeline only advances once.

closing_issues.title: Add Manual Refresh Button & Auto-Refresh (5min) to Project Board with GitHub API Rate Limit Optimization
closing_issues.body:
**User Story:**
As a project board user, I want a manual refresh button and automatic 5-minute background refresh so that I always have access to up-to-date board data without needing to reload the page. I also want a tooltip on the refresh control clearly indicating the 5-minute auto-refresh frequency so I understand the data freshness at a glance.

**Requirements:**
- System MUST add a manual refresh button to the project board UI that triggers an immediate data reload from GitHub
- System MUST implement an automatic background refresh on a 5-minute interval when the project board is active/visible
- System MUST display a tooltip on the refresh button indicating the 5-minute auto-refresh frequency (e.g., 'Auto-refreshes every 5 minutes')
- System MUST reset the 5-minute auto-refresh countdown timer whenever a manual refresh is triggered to prevent redundant consecutive API calls
- System MUST audit all existing GitHub API calls made by the project board and eliminate or consolidate any duplicate, redundant, or unnecessary requests
- System MUST implement request deduplication and/or caching so that repeated calls for the same data within a short window return cached results instead of hitting the API
- System SHOULD use conditional requests (ETag / If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since headers) where supported by the GitHub API to reduce counted API calls on unchanged data
- System SHOULD pause or skip auto-refresh when the browser tab/window is hidden (using the Page Visibility API) to avoid wasting rate limit quota while the user is not viewing the board
- System MUST display a non-intrusive error or warning indicator if a refresh fails due to hitting GitHub API rate limits, including how long until the limit resets if available from the API response headers
- System SHOULD batch or combine GitHub API requests where possible (e.g., using GraphQL or multi-resource endpoints) to minimize total call count per refresh cycle

**Technical Notes:**
Implement the 5-minute auto-refresh using a setInterval (cleared and reset on manual refresh) combined with the Page Visibility API (document.visibilitychange) to pause polling when the tab is hidden. Leverage GitHub API response headers (X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset, ETag) to implement smart caching — store ETags per resource and use conditional GET requests to receive 304 Not Modified responses that don't count against the rate limit or consume bandwidth. Consider migrating chatty REST calls to a single GitHub GraphQL query per refresh cycle to dramatically reduce the number of HTTP requests. A centralized API client/service layer should be introduced (or enhanced) to enforce deduplication, caching TTLs, and rate-limit-aware backoff logic across the entire project board feature.

mentioned_issues.title: Add Native iOS Support for iPhone 14 Pro Max
mentioned_issues.body:
**User Story:**
As a mobile user on an iPhone 14 Pro Max, I want to use this app as a native iOS application so that I can access all app functionality seamlessly on my phone with a native mobile experience, including platform-specific gestures, performance, and UI conventions.

**Requirements:**
- System MUST build and deploy the app as a native iOS application compatible with iPhone 14 Pro Max running iOS 16 and above.
- System MUST support the iPhone 14 Pro Max screen dimensions (6.7-inch, 2778×1284 @3x) with fully responsive and properly scaled layouts.
- System MUST respect iOS safe area insets, including the Dynamic Island region at the top and the home indicator area at the bottom, ensuring no UI elements are obscured.
- System MUST support iOS system Dark Mode and Light Mode, dynamically adapting the app's color scheme based on the user's system preference.
- System MUST implement native iOS navigation patterns (e.g., swipe-back gesture, tab bar, navigation stack) consistent with Apple Human Interface Guidelines.
- System MUST handle iOS app lifecycle events (foreground, background, suspend, terminate) gracefully, preserving user state where applicable.
- System SHOULD support push notifications via Apple Push Notification service (APNs) if the app includes notification functionality.
- System MUST ensure all interactive elements meet Apple's minimum touch target size of 44×44 points for accessibility and usability.
- System SHOULD be submitted to and pass Apple App Store review requirements, including compliance with App Store Guidelines and privacy manifest requirements.
- System MUST support standard iOS accessibility features including Dynamic Type font scaling, VoiceOver compatibility, and sufficient color contrast ratios.

**Technical Notes:**
This feature requires either building a new native iOS app using Swift/SwiftUI or React Native/Flutter (depending on the current tech stack), or wrapping an existing web app using a WebView-based approach (e.g., Capacitor or Cordova) as a transitional step. If the current app is React/web-based, Capacitor (Ionic) is a strong candidate for rapid native iOS packaging with access to native device APIs. An Apple Developer Program membership ($99/year) is required for App Store distribution and device testing. The Xcode build environment (macOS required) must be configured with the correct provisioning profiles and signing certificates targeting iOS 16+. Ensure the app's Info.plist includes required usage description strings for any device permissions requested (camera, notifications, location, etc.).

mentioned_issues.title: Add Manual Refresh Button & Auto-Refresh (5min) to Project Board with GitHub API Rate Limit Optimization
mentioned_issues.body:
**User Story:**
As a project board user, I want a manual refresh button and automatic 5-minute background refresh so that I always have access to up-to-date board data without needing to reload the page. I also want a tooltip on the refresh control clearly indicating the 5-minute auto-refresh frequency so I understand the data freshness at a glance.

**Requirements:**
- System MUST add a manual refresh button to the project board UI that triggers an immediate data reload from GitHub
- System MUST implement an automatic background refresh on a 5-minute interval when the project board is active/visible
- System MUST display a tooltip on the refresh button indicating the 5-minute auto-refresh frequency (e.g., 'Auto-refreshes every 5 minutes')
- System MUST reset the 5-minute auto-refresh countdown timer whenever a manual refresh is triggered to prevent redundant consecutive API calls
- System MUST audit all existing GitHub API calls made by the project board and eliminate or consolidate any duplicate, redundant, or unnecessary requests
- System MUST implement request deduplication and/or caching so that repeated calls for the same data within a short window return cached results instead of hitting the API
- System SHOULD use conditional requests (ETag / If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since headers) where supported by the GitHub API to reduce counted API calls on unchanged data
- System SHOULD pause or skip auto-refresh when the browser tab/window is hidden (using the Page Visibility API) to avoid wasting rate limit quota while the user is not viewing the board
- System MUST display a non-intrusive error or warning indicator if a refresh fails due to hitting GitHub API rate limits, including how long until the limit resets if available from the API response headers
- System SHOULD batch or combine GitHub API requests where possible (e.g., using GraphQL or multi-resource endpoints) to minimize total call count per refresh cycle

**Technical Notes:**
Implement the 5-minute auto-refresh using a setInterval (cleared and reset on manual refresh) combined with the Page Visibility API (document.visibilitychange) to pause polling when the tab is hidden. Leverage GitHub API response headers (X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset, ETag) to implement smart caching — store ETags per resource and use conditional GET requests to receive 304 Not Modified responses that don't count against the rate limit or consume bandwidth. Consider migrating chatty REST calls to a single GitHub GraphQL query per refresh cycle to dramatically reduce the number of HTTP requests. A centralized API client/service layer should be introduced (or enhanced) to enforce deduplication, caching TTLs, and rate-limit-aware backoff logic across the entire project board feature.

mentioned_issues.title: Add Native iOS Support for iPhone 14 Pro Max
mentioned_issues.body:
**User Story:**
As a mobile user on an iPhone 14 Pro Max, I want to use this app as a native iOS application so that I can access all app functionality seamlessly on my phone with a native mobile experience, including platform-specific gestures, performance, and UI conventions.

**Requirements:**
- System MUST build and deploy the app as a native iOS application compatible with iPhone 14 Pro Max running iOS 16 and above.
- System MUST support the iPhone 14 Pro Max screen dimensions (6.7-inch, 2778×1284 @3x) with fully responsive and properly scaled layouts.
- System MUST respect iOS safe area insets, including the Dynamic Island region at the top and the home indicator area at the bottom, ensuring no UI elements are obscured.
- System MUST support iOS system Dark Mode and Light Mode, dynamically adapting the app's color scheme based on the user's system preference.
- System MUST implement native iOS navigation patterns (e.g., swipe-back gesture, tab bar, navigation stack) consistent with Apple Human Interface Guidelines.
- System MUST handle iOS app lifecycle events (foreground, background, suspend, terminate) gracefully, preserving user state where applicable.
- System SHOULD support push notifications via Apple Push Notification service (APNs) if the app includes notification functionality.
- System MUST ensure all interactive elements meet Apple's minimum touch target size of 44×44 points for accessibility and usability.
- System SHOULD be submitted to and pass Apple App Store review requirements, including compliance with App Store Guidelines and privacy manifest requirements.
- System MUST support standard iOS accessibility features including Dynamic Type font scaling, VoiceOver compatibility, and sufficient color contrast ratios.

**Technical Notes:**
This feature requires either building a new native iOS app using Swift/SwiftUI or React Native/Flutter (depending on the current tech stack), or wrapping an existing web app using a WebView-based approach (e.g., Capacitor or Cordova) as a transitional step. If the current app is React/web-based, Capacitor (Ionic) is a strong candidate for rapid native iOS packaging with access to native device APIs. An Apple Developer Program membership ($99/year) is required for App Store distribution and device testing. The Xcode build environment (macOS required) must be configured with the correct provisioning profiles and signing certificates targeting iOS 16+. Ensure the app's Info.plist includes required usage description strings for any device permissions requested (camera, notifications, location, etc.).

closing_issues.title: Add Housekeeping Issue Templates with Configurable Triggers for Recurring Project Maintenance
closing_issues.body:
**User Story:**
As a project maintainer using the GitHub Workflows Project, I want to define recurring 'housekeeping' tasks (e.g., Security and Privacy Review, Test Coverage Refresh, Bug Bash) that automatically create predefined GitHub Issues with Sub Issues — defaulting to the Spec Kit reconfiguration for the agent pipeline — so that critical maintenance workflows are triggered consistently without manual intervention. I need to configure each housekeeping task with either a time-based trigger or a count-based trigger (X number of parent GitHub Issues created since the last trigger), and have each task use a stored GitHub Issue template that fans out into sub issues aligned to the project board's agent pipeline configuration.

**Requirements:**
- System MUST allow users to create named housekeeping tasks with a name, optional description, and an associated stored GitHub Issue template used to generate the parent issue upon trigger.
- System MUST support two mutually exclusive trigger modes per housekeeping task: (1) time-based trigger using a configurable schedule (e.g., daily, weekly, monthly, custom cron), and (2) count-based trigger that fires after X number of new parent GitHub Issues have been created in the project since the last trigger.
- System MUST generate sub issues for each housekeeping task based on the project board's agent pipeline configuration, defaulting to the Spec Kit reconfiguration for the agent pipeline when no custom sub issue mapping is defined.
- System MUST provide built-in pre-configured starter templates for at minimum three housekeeping task types: 'Security and Privacy Review' (reviews codebase to ensure the highest level of security, privacy, and best practices), 'Test Coverage Refresh' (increases quality testing and coverage using best practices while resolving bugs and issues), and 'Bug Bash' (reviews the codebase to find and resolve bugs and issues).
- System MUST store and manage reusable GitHub Issue templates that can be referenced by housekeeping task definitions, allowing templates to be created, edited, and deleted independently of the tasks that use them.
- System MUST track the last trigger timestamp and last trigger parent-issue-count baseline per housekeeping task to accurately evaluate count-based and time-based trigger conditions.
- System MUST allow users to manually trigger any housekeeping task on demand (a 'Run Now' action), bypassing the configured trigger condition, and record this as a triggered event in the task history.
- System MUST display a trigger/run history log per housekeeping task showing timestamp, trigger type (scheduled, count-based, manual), the resulting GitHub Issue URL, and status (success/failure).
- System SHOULD validate that the referenced GitHub Issue template and agent pipeline sub issue configuration exist and are valid before saving a housekeeping task, surfacing errors inline.
- System SHOULD support enabling and disabling individual housekeeping tasks without deleting them, preserving their configuration and history.

**Technical Notes:**
Housekeeping task definitions should be persisted in the project's configuration store (e.g., a JSON/YAML config file or database table) with fields for: id, name, description, templateRef, subIssueConfig (defaulting to Spec Kit agent pipeline reconfiguration), triggerType ('time' | 'count'), triggerValue (cron string or integer), lastTriggeredAt (ISO timestamp), lastTriggeredIssueCount (integer), enabled (boolean). The count-based trigger requires a hook into the parent issue creation event pipeline to increment and evaluate the counter atomically. Time-based triggers should integrate with the existing GitHub Actions scheduled workflow system or an internal cron scheduler. When a task fires, the system should call the GitHub Issues API to create the parent issue from the stored template, then iterate the agent pipeline sub issue configuration to create child issues linked via GitHub's sub-issue relationship (or tasklist blocks if using Projects). The three built-in types (Security & Privacy Review, Test Coverage Refresh, Bug Bash) should ship as seed templates referencing `#codebase` context for the agent pipeline to process. Ensure idempotency guards so that a task cannot be double-triggered within a minimum cooldown window.

mentioned_issues.title: Refactor Codebase: Remove Dead Code, Backwards Compatibility & Stale Tests
mentioned_issues.body:
## Overview
Perform a thorough codebase cleanup to improve maintainability and reduce technical debt. This involves removing backwards compatibility shims, eliminating dead code paths, consolidating duplicated logic, and deleting stale/irrelevant tests. The goal is a leaner, simpler, and more idiomatic codebase.

## Technical Details
- Identify and remove backwards compatibility layers, legacy shims, and deprecated code paths that are no longer needed
- Hunt down dead code (unreachable branches, unused variables, functions, imports, and exports)
- Consolidate duplicated logic following DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principles
- Apply language/framework best practices where existing code deviates from modern standards
- Remove stale, redundant, or obsolete tests that no longer reflect current behavior or test non-existent functionality
- Ensure no regressions are introduced — all remaining tests must pass after cleanup
- Review related documentation or inline comments that may also be outdated

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All backwards compatibility code and legacy shims are removed with no remaining references
- [ ] Dead code (unused functions, variables, imports, unreachable branches) is fully eliminated
- [ ] Duplicated logic is consolidated into shared, reusable abstractions
- [ ] Stale and obsolete tests are removed; all remaining tests pass cleanly
- [ ] Code follows current best practices and passes linting/formatting checks with no new violations

mentioned_issues.title: Add Blue Background Color to App
mentioned_issues.body:
## Original Request

> add blue background to app

## User Story

As a user of the application, I want the app to have a blue background so that the visual appearance is updated to reflect the desired color scheme. This change should apply consistently across the app's primary background surfaces.

## UI/UX Description

Apply a blue background color to the main application shell or root container. The specific shade of blue should align with the existing design system or brand palette (e.g., a primary blue such as #1E90FF, #0057B7, or a Tailwind/Material blue token if one exists). The background should render consistently across all screen sizes (mobile, tablet, desktop) and not interfere with text legibility — ensure sufficient contrast ratio (WCAG AA minimum 4.5:1) between the blue background and any foreground text or icons. If the app uses light/dark mode, define the blue background behavior for both themes. The change should be applied at the top-level layout or global CSS/style file to propagate uniformly without requiring per-component overrides.

## Functional Requirements

- System MUST apply a blue background color to the root/top-level application container so it is visible on every page and route.
- System MUST use a specific blue color value consistent with the project's existing design system, brand guidelines, or CSS variable tokens (e.g., a defined blue hex, RGB, or named token).
- System MUST maintain a WCAG AA-compliant contrast ratio (minimum 4.5:1) between the blue background and all overlaid text, icons, and UI elements.
- System MUST render the blue background consistently across all supported screen sizes and breakpoints (mobile, tablet, desktop).
- System SHOULD define the blue background via a global stylesheet, CSS variable, or theme configuration file rather than inline styles to ensure maintainability and easy future updates.
- System SHOULD handle light and dark mode variants — either applying the blue background in both modes or scoping it appropriately to the active theme.
- System MUST NOT cause any existing UI components (cards, modals, navbars, buttons) to become unreadable or visually broken as a result of the background color change.
- System SHOULD update or add a Storybook story, design token, or visual regression snapshot (if applicable) to reflect the new background color.

## Technical Notes

Locate the root layout component or global CSS file (e.g., `App.tsx`, `_app.tsx`, `index.css`, `globals.css`, or equivalent) and apply the blue background via a CSS class, inline style, or theme token update. If the project uses a design system (Tailwind CSS, MUI, Chakra UI, etc.), prefer using an existing blue token (e.g., `bg-blue-600` in Tailwind, `primary.main` in MUI) rather than a hardcoded hex value to stay consistent with the design system. If no design system is present, define a CSS variable `--color-app-bg: #1E90FF` (or appropriate blue) in `:root` and reference it in the background property. Verify no z-index or stacking context issues cause the background to be obscured by overlapping elements.

closing_issues.title: Improve Logging, Error Message Handling & Code Quality via Full Code Review
closing_issues.body:
## Original Request

> Improve logging and error message handling. Use best practices. Ensure logs are sanitized. Perform full code review. Keep code simple and DRY.

## User Story

As a developer maintaining this codebase, I want logging and error message handling to follow best practices — including log sanitization, DRY principles, and simplified code — so that the system is more secure, easier to debug, and maintainable long-term.

## UI/UX Description

No direct end-user UI changes are expected; however, internal tooling, dashboards, or log viewers consuming these logs should receive cleaner, consistently structured log output (e.g., structured JSON logs with standard severity levels). Error messages surfaced to end users must be sanitized to never expose sensitive data (PII, stack traces, secrets, internal paths). Developer-facing log output should be human-readable in local environments and machine-parseable (structured) in production.

## Functional Requirements

- System MUST sanitize all log output to strip sensitive data including PII, credentials, secrets, tokens, and internal file paths before writing to any log sink
- System MUST use a consistent, structured logging format (e.g., JSON with fields: timestamp, level, message, context) across all modules and services
- System MUST apply standardized log severity levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL) correctly and consistently — e.g., caught-and-handled errors must not be logged as FATAL
- System MUST eliminate duplicated logging and error-handling logic by extracting shared utilities or middleware (DRY principle)
- System MUST ensure error messages returned to callers or end users do not leak internal implementation details, stack traces, or raw database/system errors
- System SHOULD perform a full code review pass to identify and remove dead code, overly complex logic, and inconsistent patterns in logging and error handling
- System MUST ensure all unhandled exceptions and promise rejections are caught and logged with sufficient context (e.g., request ID, user ID if safe, operation name) for debuggability
- System SHOULD add or update unit/integration tests to verify that sanitized, correctly leveled logs are emitted for key success, warning, and error paths
- System MUST ensure no secrets or API keys are ever interpolated into log messages, enforced via static analysis or linting rules where possible

## Technical Notes

Conduct a full code review targeting all logger instantiation sites, error catch blocks, and error response serializers. Introduce or enforce a centralized logging utility/wrapper (e.g., a logger module or middleware) to eliminate ad-hoc console.log or scattered logger calls — this is the primary DRY refactor target. Implement a log-sanitization layer (e.g., a redact function or a library like 'pino-noir' for Node.js or equivalent) that scrubs sensitive fields before log emission. Consider adopting a structured logging library appropriate to the stack (e.g., Pino, Winston, Loguru, Zap) if not already in use, and enforce consistent usage via linting rules or code review guidelines.

mentioned_issues.body:
## Bug Bash: Full Codebase Review & Fix

### Objective
Perform a comprehensive bug bash code review of the **entire codebase**. Identify bugs, fix them, and ensure fixes are validated by tests.

### Scope — Review Categories
Audit every file in the repository for the following bug categories, in priority order:

1. **Security vulnerabilities** — auth bypasses, injection risks, secrets/tokens exposed in code or config, insecure defaults, improper input validation
2. **Runtime errors** — unhandled exceptions, race conditions, null/None references, missing imports, type errors, file handle leaks, database connection leaks
3. **Logic bugs** — incorrect state transitions, wrong API calls, off-by-one errors, data inconsistencies, broken control flow, incorrect return values
4. **Test gaps & test quality** — untested code paths, tests that pass for the wrong reason, mock leaks (e.g., `MagicMock` objects leaking into production paths like database file paths), assertions that never fail, missing edge case coverage
5. **Code quality issues** — dead code, unreachable branches, duplicated logic, hardcoded values that should be configurable, missing error messages, silent failures

### Actions Required

**For obvious/clear bugs:**
- Fix the bug directly in the source code.
- Update any existing tests that are affected by the fix.
- Add at least one new regression test per bug to ensure it does not reoccur.
- Write a clear commit message explaining: what the bug was, why it's a bug, and how the fix resolves it.

**For ambiguous or trade-off situations:**
- Do NOT make the change.
- Instead, add a `# TODO(bug-bash):` comment at the relevant location describing the issue, the options, and why it needs a human decision.
- Include these in a summary (see Output below).

### Validation
After all fixes are applied:
1. Run `pytest` and ensure the full test suite passes (including all new regression tests).
2. Run any existing linting/formatting checks if configured (e.g., `flake8`, `black`, `ruff`).
3. Do not commit if tests fail — iterate on the fix until green.

### Output
At the end, provide a single summary comment with:

mentioned_issues.title: Add Chat History Navigation: Up/Down Arrow Key Cycling Through Previously Sent Messages
mentioned_issues.body:
## Original Request

> Update app chat experience with useful chat features, like saved chat history - if the user hits the up arrow button, it should step through previously sent messages so the user can easily send the same messages without retyping.

## User Story

As a chat user, I want to press the up arrow key in the chat input field to step backward through my previously sent messages so that I can quickly resend or edit past messages without retyping them. I also want to press the down arrow key to step forward through history (toward the most recent message), and pressing down past the newest entry should restore any in-progress draft I had before navigating.

## UI/UX Description

The chat input field should respond to keyboard navigation in a manner consistent with terminal/shell history UX conventions. When the input field is focused and empty (or the cursor is at the start of the input), pressing the Up Arrow key cycles backward through previously sent messages, populating the input field with each historical message one step at a time. Pressing Down Arrow cycles forward through the history toward the most recent entry; pressing Down past the last history entry restores the original in-progress draft (if any). The history navigation should feel instantaneous with no visible loading state. A subtle visual indicator (e.g., a faint history icon or italicized text color change) may optionally signal to the user that the input is showing a historical message vs. a new draft. If the user edits a historical message while navigating, the edited version should NOT overwrite the stored history — it should only be persisted to history upon successful send. On mobile or touch devices, the up/down arrow feature is inherently keyboard-driven and should gracefully degrade (feature is only active when a hardware keyboard is present). The history should persist across page refreshes and sessions using localStorage or equivalent client-side storage.

## Functional Requirements

- System MUST capture and store every successfully sent chat message in an ordered history list, appended in chronological order upon send.
- System MUST respond to the Up Arrow keydown event in the chat input field by replacing the current input value with the previous message in history, stepping one entry further back on each successive Up Arrow press.
- System MUST respond to the Down Arrow keydown event in the chat input field by stepping forward through history; when the history pointer moves past the most recent entry, the input MUST restore the user's pre-navigation draft (even if it was an empty string).
- System MUST save the user's current in-progress draft before history navigation begins, so it can be restored when the user navigates back past the newest history entry with the Down Arrow key.
- System MUST NOT overwrite stored history entries when a user edits a recalled historical message — edits only persist to history if the edited message is actually sent.
- System MUST persist chat history to localStorage (or equivalent client-side storage) so that history survives page refreshes and browser session restores.
- System SHOULD cap stored history at a configurable maximum (e.g., 100 most recent messages) to prevent unbounded localStorage growth, evicting the oldest entry when the cap is reached.
- System MUST only intercept Up/Down Arrow keydown events for history navigation when the chat input field is focused, to avoid conflicting with other keyboard interactions on the page.
- System SHOULD deduplicate consecutive identical messages in history (e.g., sending the same message twice in a row should only add one history entry) to keep the history list clean and useful.
- System MUST reset the history navigation pointer back to the 'newest' position (beyond the last entry) whenever the user successfully sends a message.

## Technical Notes

Implement a custom React hook (e.g., `useChatHistory`) that manages the history array, the current navigation index, and the draft buffer in component state, with a `useEffect` syncing history to `localStorage` on every update. Attach a `keydown` event handler (or use React's `onKeyDown`) to the chat input element, intercepting `ArrowUp` and `ArrowDown` keys and calling `preventDefault()` to stop the cursor from jumping to the start/end of the input text. Use a sentinel index value (e.g., `-1` or `history.length`) to represent the 'draft' position beyond history bounds. For the localStorage key, namespace it per-user or per-chat-room if the app supports multiple conversations. Ensure the history hook is decoupled from the UI component so it can be unit-tested independently.

> Update app chat experience with useful chat features, like saved chat history - if the user hits the up arrow button, it should step through previously sent messages so the user can easily send the same messages without retyping.

## User Story

As a chat user, I want to press the up arrow key in the chat input field to step backward through my previously sent messages so that I can quickly resend or edit past messages without retyping them. I also want to press the down arrow key to step forward through history (toward the most recent message), and pressing down past the newest entry should restore any in-progress draft I had before navigating.

## UI/UX Description

The chat input field should respond to keyboard navigation in a manner consistent with terminal/shell history UX conventions. When the input field is focused and empty (or the cursor is at the start of the input), pressing the Up Arrow key cycles backward through previously sent messages, populating the input field with each historical message one step at a time. Pressing Down Arrow cycles forward through the history toward the most recent entry; pressing Down past the last history entry restores the original in-progress draft (if any). The history navigation should feel instantaneous with no visible loading state. A subtle visual indicator (e.g., a faint history icon or italicized text color change) may optionally signal to the user that the input is showing a historical message vs. a new draft. If the user edits a historical message while navigating, the edited version should NOT overwrite the stored history — it should only be persisted to history upon successful send. On mobile or touch devices, the up/down arrow feature is inherently keyboard-driven and should gracefully degrade (feature is only active when a hardware keyboard is present). The history should persist across page refreshes and sessions using localStorage or equivalent client-side storage.

## Functional Requirements

- System MUST capture and store every successfully sent chat message in an ordered history list, appended in chronological order upon send.
- System MUST respond to the Up Arrow keydown event in the chat input field by replacing the current input value with the previous message in history, stepping one entry further back on each successive Up Arrow press.
- System MUST respond to the Down Arrow keydown event in the chat input field by stepping forward through history; when the history pointer moves past the most recent entry, the input MUST restore the user's pre-navigation draft (even if it was an empty string).
- System MUST save the user's current in-progress draft before history navigation begins, so it can be restored when the user navigates back past the newest history entry with the Down Arrow key.
- System MUST NOT overwrite stored history entries when a user edits a recalled historical message — edits only persist to history if the edited message is actually sent.
- System MUST persist chat history to localStorage (or equivalent client-side storage) so that history survives page refreshes and browser session restores.
- System SHOULD cap stored history at a configurable maximum (e.g., 100 most recent messages) to prevent unbounded localStorage growth, evicting the oldest entry when the cap is reached.
- System MUST only intercept Up/Down Arrow keydown events for history navigation when the chat input field is focused, to avoid conflicting with other keyboard interactions on the page.
- System SHOULD deduplicate consecutive identical messages in history (e.g., sending the same message twice in a row should only add one history entry) to keep the history list clean and useful.
- System MUST reset the history navigation pointer back to the 'newest' position (beyond the last entry) whenever the user successfully sends a message.

## Technical Notes

Implement a custom React hook (e.g., `useChatHistory`) that manages the history array, the current navigation index, and the draft buffer in component state, with a `useEffect` syncing history to `localStorage` on every update. Attach a `keydown` event handler (or use React's `onKeyDown`) to the chat input element, intercepting `ArrowUp` and `ArrowDown` keys and calling `preventDefault()` to stop the cursor from jumping to the start/end of the input text. Use a sentinel index value (e.g., `-1` or `history.length`) to represent the 'draft' position beyond history bounds. For the localStorage key, namespace it per-user or per-chat-room if the app supports multiple conversations. Ensure the history hook is decoupled from the UI component so it can be unit-tested independently.

mentioned_issues.title: Bug Basher
mentioned_issues.body:
## Bug Bash: Full Codebase Review & Fix

### Objective
Perform a comprehensive bug bash code review of the **entire codebase**. Identify bugs, fix them, and ensure fixes are validated by tests.

### Scope — Review Categories
Audit every file in the repository for the following bug categories, in priority order:

1. **Security vulnerabilities** — auth bypasses, injection risks, secrets/tokens exposed in code or config, insecure defaults, improper input validation
2. **Runtime errors** — unhandled exceptions, race conditions, null/None references, missing imports, type errors, file handle leaks, database connection leaks
3. **Logic bugs** — incorrect state transitions, wrong API calls, off-by-one errors, data inconsistencies, broken control flow, incorrect return values
4. **Test gaps & test quality** — untested code paths, tests that pass for the wrong reason, mock leaks (e.g., `MagicMock` objects leaking into production paths like database file paths), assertions that never fail, missing edge case coverage
5. **Code quality issues** — dead code, unreachable branches, duplicated logic, hardcoded values that should be configurable, missing error messages, silent failures

### Actions Required

**For obvious/clear bugs:**
- Fix the bug directly in the source code.
- Update any existing tests that are affected by the fix.
- Add at least one new regression test per bug to ensure it does not reoccur.
- Write a clear commit message explaining: what the bug was, why it's a bug, and how the fix resolves it.

**For ambiguous or trade-off situations:**
- Do NOT make the change.
- Instead, add a `# TODO(bug-bash):` comment at the relevant location describing the issue, the options, and why it needs a human decision.
- Include these in a summary (see Output below).

### Validation
After all fixes are applied:
1. Run `pytest` and ensure the full test suite passes (including all new regression tests).
2. Run any existing linting/formatting checks if configured (e.g., `flake8`, `black`, `ruff`).
3. Do not commit if tests fail — iterate on the fix until green.

### Output
At the end, provide a single summary comment with:

| # | File | Line(s) | Category | Description | Status |
|---|------|---------|----------|-------------|--------|
| 1 | `path/to/file.py` | 42-45 | Security | Description of bug | ✅ Fixed |
| 2 | `path/to/file.py` | 100 | Logic | Description of ambiguity | ⚠️ Flagged (TODO) |

- **✅ Fixed** — bug was resolved, tests added, all passing
- **⚠️ Flagged (TODO)** — ambiguous issue left as `TODO(bug-bash)` comment for human review

### Constraints
- Do not change the project's architecture or public API surface.
- Do not add new dependencies.
- Preserve existing code style and patterns.
- Each fix should be minimal and focused — no drive-by refactors.
- If a file has no bugs, skip it — don't mention it in the summary.

mentioned_issues.title: Enhance #help and General # Commands with Robust, Best-Practice Chat UX
mentioned_issues.body:
## Original Request

> Update to provide more robust chat #help and general # commands details for a better user experience. Use best practices.

## User Story

As a chat user interacting with the GitHub Workflows Project, I want the #help command and all general # (slash/hash) commands to provide richer, clearer, and more comprehensive guidance so that I can quickly discover available commands, understand their usage, and complete workflows without confusion or trial-and-error.

## UI/UX Description

The #help response should display a well-structured, scannable list of all available # commands grouped by category (e.g., General, Workflow, Notifications). Each command entry should include the command name (bold/highlighted), a concise one-line description, and a usage example with optional parameters shown in brackets. A summary header should confirm context (e.g., 'Here are all available commands for this channel'). Individual # command responses should include inline usage hints when invoked incorrectly or without required arguments, rather than silent failures. All responses should use consistent formatting (e.g., code blocks for command syntax, emoji or icons for visual scanning where supported), follow a progressive disclosure pattern (short summary first, expandable details), and be accessible — avoiding reliance on color alone to convey meaning. On mobile/narrow viewports, the layout should remain readable without horizontal scrolling.

## Functional Requirements

- System MUST provide a #help command that returns a complete, categorized list of all available # commands in the chat interface
- System MUST display each command in #help output with its name, a short description, and a syntax/usage example including optional and required parameters
- System MUST follow best practices for chat command UX, including consistent prefix conventions, predictable response formatting, and inline error guidance
- System MUST show context-sensitive usage hints when a # command is invoked with missing required arguments or incorrect syntax, rather than returning a generic error or no response
- System MUST ensure all # command responses use consistent visual formatting (e.g., code blocks for syntax, grouped sections with headers) across all supported chat clients
- System SHOULD support a shorthand variant (e.g., #help <command>) that returns detailed documentation for a single specific command
- System SHOULD include a 'Did you mean…?' suggestion when an unrecognized # command is entered that closely matches a valid command name
- System MUST ensure all #help and # command output is accessible, avoiding color as the sole differentiator and maintaining readability in both light and dark themes
- System SHOULD log usage of #help and # commands to enable analytics on which commands are most/least discovered, informing future UX improvements

## Technical Notes

Audit all existing # command handlers to inventory current descriptions, parameter schemas, and error paths before making changes — this is the source of truth for the help content. Implement a centralized command registry (e.g., a JSON/YAML manifest or code-level decorator pattern) where each command self-documents its name, aliases, description, parameters, and examples, so #help output is always auto-generated and never stale. Apply fuzzy matching (e.g., Levenshtein distance) for 'Did you mean?' suggestions on unrecognized commands. Ensure the help formatter respects the rendering capabilities of the target chat platform (e.g., Markdown in GitHub, plain text fallback elsewhere) and validate output against WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility guidelines.

mentioned_issues.body:
## Bug Bash: Full Codebase Review & Fix

### Objective
Perform a comprehensive bug bash code review of the **entire codebase**. Identify bugs, fix them, and ensure fixes are validated by tests.

### Scope — Review Categories
Audit every file in the repository for the following bug categories, in priority order:

1. **Security vulnerabilities** — auth bypasses, injection risks, secrets/tokens exposed in code or config, insecure defaults, improper input validation
2. **Runtime errors** — unhandled exceptions, race conditions, null/None references, missing imports, type errors, file handle leaks, database connection leaks
3. **Logic bugs** — incorrect state transitions, wrong API calls, off-by-one errors, data inconsistencies, broken control flow, incorrect return values
4. **Test gaps & test quality** — untested code paths, tests that pass for the wrong reason, mock leaks (e.g., `MagicMock` objects leaking into production paths like database file paths), assertions that never fail, missing edge case coverage
5. **Code quality issues** — dead code, unreachable branches, duplicated logic, hardcoded values that should be configurable, missing error messages, silent failures

### Actions Required

**For obvious/clear bugs:**
- Fix the bug directly in the source code.
- Update any existing tests that are affected by the fix.
- Add at least one new regression test per bug to ensure it does not reoccur.
- Write a clear commit message explaining: what the bug was, why it's a bug, and how the fix resolves it.

**For ambiguous or trade-off situations:**
- Do NOT make the change.
- Instead, add a `# TODO(bug-bash):` comment at the relevant location describing the issue, the options, and why it needs a human decision.
- Include these in a summary (see Output below).

### Validation
After all fixes are applied:
1. Run `pytest` and ensure the full test suite passes (including all new regression tests).
2. Run any existing linting/formatting checks if configured (e.g., `flake8`, `black`, `ruff`).
3. Do not commit if tests fail — iterate on the fix until green.

### Output
At the end, provide a single summary comment with:

| # | File | Line(s) | Category | Description | Status |
|---|------|---------|----------|-------------|--------|

- **⚠️ Flagged (TODO)** — ambiguous issue left as `TODO(bug-bash)` comment for human review

- Do not change the project's architecture or public API surface.
- Do not add new dependencies.
- Preserve existing code style and patterns.
- Each fix should be minimal and focused — no drive-by refactors.
- If a file has no bugs, skip it — don't mention it in the summary.

mentioned_issues.title: Add Chat Message History Navigation with Up Arrow Key Support
mentioned_issues.body:
## Original Request

> Update app chat experience with useful chat features, like saved chat history - if the user hits the up arrow button, it should step through previously sent messages so the user can easily send the same messages without retyping.

## User Story

As a chat user, I want to be able to press the up arrow key in the chat input to step through my previously sent messages so that I can quickly resend or reuse past messages without retyping them. This mirrors the familiar terminal/shell history navigation pattern, reducing friction for repetitive or follow-up interactions.

## UI/UX Description

The chat input field should support keyboard-driven history navigation: pressing the Up Arrow key cycles backward through previously sent messages (most recent first), populating the input field with each historical message. Pressing the Down Arrow key cycles forward through history, returning toward the most recent entry, and pressing Down past the most recent history entry restores any in-progress draft the user had typed before navigating. The input cursor should be positioned at the end of the restored message text. Visual feedback (e.g., subtle highlight or border change on the input) may indicate history-navigation mode. On mobile or touch devices, a dedicated 'history' button or swipe gesture should be considered as an alternative to the keyboard shortcut. History should persist across page refreshes/sessions (stored locally), and the list of saved messages should be bounded to a reasonable maximum (e.g., 50–100 entries) to avoid unbounded storage growth.

## Functional Requirements

- System MUST save each successfully sent chat message to a persistent local history store (e.g., localStorage or IndexedDB), ordered chronologically with the most recent message last.
- System MUST allow the user to press the Up Arrow key while the chat input field is focused to populate the input with the previously sent message, stepping further back through history on each successive Up Arrow press.
- System MUST allow the user to press the Down Arrow key while in history-navigation mode to move forward (more recent) through history, and when advancing past the most recent history entry, the system MUST restore any unsaved draft text the user had in the input before beginning navigation.
- System MUST position the text cursor at the end of the restored message text whenever a history entry is loaded into the input field.
- System MUST cap the stored history at a configurable maximum number of entries (default: 100), automatically removing the oldest entry when the cap is exceeded.
- System MUST persist chat history across browser sessions so that history is available after page refresh or app reload.
- System SHOULD deduplicate consecutive identical messages in history (i.e., sending the same message twice in a row should not create two adjacent identical history entries).
- System MUST NOT trigger history navigation when the Up/Down Arrow keys are pressed inside a multi-line input while the cursor is not on the first/last line respectively, preserving normal cursor movement within multi-line text.
- System SHOULD provide a mechanism to clear chat history (e.g., a settings option or a dedicated clear-history button), and MUST confirm with the user before permanently deleting history.
- System MUST handle an empty history gracefully — pressing Up Arrow when no history exists should produce no change to the input field.

## Technical Notes

Implement a custom React hook (e.g., `useChatHistory`) or equivalent framework utility that manages the history array and the current navigation index as state. Use `localStorage` for persistence (JSON-serialized array); migrate to `IndexedDB` if history payloads grow large or if multi-tab sync is required. Attach `onKeyDown` handlers to the chat input element to intercept Arrow key events, calling `event.preventDefault()` to suppress default cursor movement only when navigation is valid (i.e., Up while index > 0, Down while in navigation mode). Store an ephemeral 'draft' value when the user first presses Up so it can be restored on Down-past-end. If the input is a `<textarea>` (multi-line), check `selectionStart`/`selectionEnd` and the presence of newlines to determine whether the cursor is on the first or last line before activating history navigation, to avoid conflicting with normal multi-line cursor movement.

mentioned_issues.title: Add Chat Message History Navigation with Up Arrow Key Support
mentioned_issues.body:
## Original Request

> Update app chat experience with useful chat features, like saved chat history - if the user hits the up arrow button, it should step through previously sent messages so the user can easily send the same messages without retyping.

## User Story

As a chat user, I want to be able to press the up arrow key in the chat input to step through my previously sent messages so that I can quickly resend or reuse past messages without retyping them. This mirrors the familiar terminal/shell history navigation pattern, reducing friction for repetitive or follow-up interactions.

## UI/UX Description

The chat input field should support keyboard-driven history navigation: pressing the Up Arrow key cycles backward through previously sent messages (most recent first), populating the input field with each historical message. Pressing the Down Arrow key cycles forward through history, returning toward the most recent entry, and pressing Down past the most recent history entry restores any in-progress draft the user had typed before navigating. The input cursor should be positioned at the end of the restored message text. Visual feedback (e.g., subtle highlight or border change on the input) may indicate history-navigation mode. On mobile or touch devices, a dedicated 'history' button or swipe gesture should be considered as an alternative to the keyboard shortcut. History should persist across page refreshes/sessions (stored locally), and the list of saved messages should be bounded to a reasonable maximum (e.g., 50–100 entries) to avoid unbounded storage growth.

## Functional Requirements

- System MUST save each successfully sent chat message to a persistent local history store (e.g., localStorage or IndexedDB), ordered chronologically with the most recent message last.
- System MUST allow the user to press the Up Arrow key while the chat input field is focused to populate the input with the previously sent message, stepping further back through history on each successive Up Arrow press.
- System MUST allow the user to press the Down Arrow key while in history-navigation mode to move forward (more recent) through history, and when advancing past the most recent history entry, the system MUST restore any unsaved draft text the user had in the input before beginning navigation.
- System MUST position the text cursor at the end of the restored message text whenever a history entry is loaded into the input field.
- System MUST cap the stored history at a configurable maximum number of entries (default: 100), automatically removing the oldest entry when the cap is exceeded.
- System MUST persist chat history across browser sessions so that history is available after page refresh or app reload.
- System SHOULD deduplicate consecutive identical messages in history (i.e., sending the same message twice in a row should not create two adjacent identical history entries).
- System MUST NOT trigger history navigation when the Up/Down Arrow keys are pressed inside a multi-line input while the cursor is not on the first/last line respectively, preserving normal cursor movement within multi-line text.
- System SHOULD provide a mechanism to clear chat history (e.g., a settings option or a dedicated clear-history button), and MUST confirm with the user before permanently deleting history.
- System MUST handle an empty history gracefully — pressing Up Arrow when no history exists should produce no change to the input field.

## Technical Notes

Implement a custom React hook (e.g., `useChatHistory`) or equivalent framework utility that manages the history array and the current navigation index as state. Use `localStorage` for persistence (JSON-serialized array); migrate to `IndexedDB` if history payloads grow large or if multi-tab sync is required. Attach `onKeyDown` handlers to the chat input element to intercept Arrow key events, calling `event.preventDefault()` to suppress default cursor movement only when navigation is valid (i.e., Up while index > 0, Down while in navigation mode). Store an ephemeral 'draft' value when the user first presses Up so it can be restored on Down-past-end. If the input is a `<textarea>` (multi-line), check `selectionStart`/`selectionEnd` and the presence of newlines to determine whether the cursor is on the first or last line before activating history navigation, to avoid conflicting with normal multi-line cursor movement.
